title: The Commoner’s Response: Building Freedom from the Ground Up | Daniel Mentz
description:
THE AMERICAN COMMONER — 250 YEARS LATER

THE COMMONER’S RESPONSE
Featuring Daniel Mentz

After inheritance, grievances, and fracture comes responsibility.

The Declaration of Independence entrusted ordinary people with an extraordinary proposition: human beings are capable of governing themselves. That principle carries a corresponding duty. When institutions fail, communities fracture, or liberty is threatened, a self-governing people must be capable of producing remedies.

The Commoner’s Response, the fourth segment of Commoner Law Group’s twelve-hour Independence Day gathering, turns deliberately toward solutions.

Daniel Mentz of Sacred Honor Educational Fellowship begins with the practical question: What can people do now? He describes the legal and private-organization pathways his fellowship teaches, including national-status work, trusts, private membership associations, ministries, equity principles, and land-related remedies. He presents these approaches as ways people can seek greater privacy, autonomy, and responsibility within the legal and institutional reality they inhabit. (Learn more and download your free e-book here: "National Status & Passport"
https://www.sacredhonoref.com/the-status-awakening#a_aid=136&a_bid=16fc02c1)

Daniel also describes the intellectual journey that led him toward the broader Exit & Build philosophy: withdraw energy from systems you regard as corrupt or destructive and invest it instead in parallel systems that support voluntary exchange, local food, private association, decentralized technology, alternative currencies, independent education, and communities of people deliberately building the lives they want to live.

Clint identifies several distinct strategic responses Americans are already pursuing:
- Stay and fix. Work within existing political and civic institutions, especially locally, to restore accountability and lawful government.
- Exit and build. Create parallel institutions and communities capable of supporting greater independence from existing systems.
- Withdraw consent. Refuse participation wherever conscience and circumstances permit, with the expectation that widespread nonparticipation can weaken illegitimate systems.
- Hold power accountable. Investigate wrongdoing, expose corruption, enforce lawful limits, and demand consequences when public actors violate their duties.

Each strategy rests upon a different judgment about what remains possible. The conversation does not require every commoner to adopt the same remedy. It asks something more fundamental: What responsibility follows from your own understanding of the problem?

A deeper issue emerges as the discussion turns toward intentional communities and parallel institutions. Building food systems, currencies, private associations, land projects, and alternative economies solves only part of the problem. Human beings eventually disagree. Accusations arise. Trust breaks. Communities that aspire to self-government therefore need institutions capable of discovering truth and resolving conflict.

Clint explains that the ancient jury principle belongs near the center of any serious project of self-government. A healthy community must know how to move from harm to accusation, from accusation to investigation and evidence, from evidence to deliberation, and ultimately toward a judgment the community can trust. Without a credible process for resolving disputes, even communities founded upon liberty can fracture from within. (Watch the full video here: "Why Freedom Movements Fall Apart and How the Jury Principle Can Help" https://youtu.be/OPyh1dNpT44)

That exchange produces one of the most important conclusions of the day:
Freedom requires more than escape from bad government. It requires competence in governing ourselves.

The American Commoner therefore faces a practical challenge 250 years after the Declaration: learn the principles, examine the remedies, understand their assumptions and risks, choose responsibly, and build institutions worthy of free people.

This is The Commoner’s Response.
